title: The slain Lamb (Revelation 5)
hook: the lion of Judah turns out to be a Lamb that was slain

segments.voice: Yesterday, the throne room: a rainbow like emerald, a sea of glass, creatures who never stop singing. Your line was holy, holy, holy. What did you stay with long enough to call it holy? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

Someone is crying in the throne room. Not a creature. Not an elder. John. In the right hand of the one on the throne is a scroll, written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals. A strong angel calls out with a loud voice: "Who is worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof?" No one in heaven, no one on earth, no one under the earth can do it. And John writes, "I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open and to read the book." Then one of the elders leans over and tells him to stop crying, and to look.

First, what John hears. The elder says: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book." A lion, and a king's titles. The lion reaches back to Jacob's blessing, where Judah is called a lion's whelp. John is told to expect power. Second, what John sees. He looks, and the King James words are: "and, lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain." He hears lion. He sees lamb. Wounded, and still standing, right at the center of the room we stood in yesterday. It has seven horns and seven eyes, and the text says the eyes are the seven Spirits of God. But the first thing the text says about the Lamb is the wound. Third, the song. The creatures and elders fall down and sing a new song: "Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain." Not worthy in spite of being slain. Worthy because of it. Christians read the Lamb as Jesus, crucified and risen, the one John the Baptist pointed to: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." Fourth, why it matters. Revelation is full of beasts and dragons and armies. But the one at the center of the throne room, the one who can open what no one else can, isn't the loudest or the fiercest. It's a lamb that was killed and stands anyway. In this book, that's what the lion looks like.
screen: `HE SEES: A LAMB, AS IT HAD BEEN SLAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find strength in gentleness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a moment coming up today where you'd usually push: an argument, a deadline, a person who tests you. Picture yourself walking into it the way a lamb would. Not weak. Steady, open-handed, without a fight to prove. Notice how much strength that would actually take. Let your shoulders drop. Let your jaw loosen. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God and simply ask for gentleness in it. If you don't, just rehearse it gently in your mind. The bell holds the time.
The slain Lamb. Announced as a lion, seen as a lamb that was killed and still stands, and found worthy to open the scroll because it was slain.
Your line: the lamb is the lion. Today, in one moment where you'd usually push, take the gentle way, and notice what strength it takes. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Christians call Jesus the Lamb of God in worship and prayer; in some forms of the communion service the words 'Lamb of God' (the Agnus Dei) are sung or said before the bread and cup are shared.

original.note: Greek: lamb. the word Revelation uses for the Lamb in chapter 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: the lion and the lamb are two different animals in the story.
what it means: John is told of a lion, looks, and sees a lamb that was slain. they are the same one.
what a scholar hears: the Lion of Juda echoes Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49:9; the slain Lamb echoes John 1:29, and the song calls it worthy for being slain.
